title: Binary Search
problemStatement: Given a sorted (ascending) array of distinct integers nums and a target value, return the index of target if it exists in the array, or -1 otherwise. Write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime.
constraints: nums is sorted in ascending order with distinct values
approachSteps: A linear scan is O(n) — sortedness lets you eliminate half the remaining search space on every comparison instead.
Track a search range with left and right bounds, initially the whole array.
Check the middle element of the current range.
If it equals target, you're done. If it's smaller than target, the answer (if any) must be to the right, so move left past the middle. If it's larger, move right before the middle.
Repeat until the range is empty (left > right), meaning the target isn't present.
optimalApproach: Classic binary search: repeatedly halve the search range based on comparing the middle element to target.
timeComplexity: O(log n) — the search range halves on every iteration.
spaceComplexity: O(1) iterative; O(log n) if written recursively (call stack).
followUps: Why is mid = left + (right - left) // 2 preferred over (left + right) // 2 in languages with fixed-width integers?
How would you adapt this to find the first or last occurrence of a target in an array with duplicates?

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problemStatement: You are given an integer array nums, sorted in ascending order (with distinct values), which has possibly been rotated at an unknown pivot. Given target, return its index, or -1 if it's not present. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime.
approachSteps: The array isn't fully sorted anymore, but here's the key insight: at any midpoint, AT LEAST ONE of the two halves (left-of-mid or right-of-mid) is still guaranteed to be normally sorted.
Find mid and check: if nums[left] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted; otherwise the right half is sorted.
Whichever half is sorted, check if target falls within that half's value range using a normal comparison — if it does, recurse/continue into that half; if not, it must be in the other half.
Repeat this halving, always working out which side is 'normal' and whether the target could be there, until found or the range is empty.
optimalApproach: Modified binary search: at each step determine which half is properly sorted, then check if the target lies in that half's range to decide which side to continue into.
timeComplexity: O(log n) — still halves the search range every step, just with an extra branch to figure out which half is sorted.
followUps: What changes if the array can contain duplicate values (this breaks the 'which half is sorted' check in some cases)?
How would you find the minimum element in a rotated sorted array using the same idea?

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problemStatement: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2 of size m and n, return the median of the two sorted arrays combined. The overall run time complexity should be O(log(min(m,n))).
approachSteps: Merging both arrays and finding the middle is O(m+n), which is straightforward but doesn't meet the O(log(min(m,n))) requirement — you need to avoid touching most of the elements.

The median splits the combined array into a left half and right half of (nearly) equal size — reframe the problem as: find a partition point in EACH array such that combined, the left parts have exactly half the total elements, and every element on the left is <= every element on the right.
Binary search on the partition index of the SMALLER array (this is why it's log of the min, not the sum) — the partition of the larger array is then determined by the total-half-size constraint.
For a candidate partition, check the boundary condition: the max of the left parts must be <= the min of the right parts on both arrays.
If the boundary condition fails because the smaller array's left part is too big, move the partition left; if too small, move it right — binary search until the condition holds.
Once the correct partition is found, the median is derived directly from the four boundary values (accounting for odd/even total length).

bruteForce.approach: Merge both arrays (or merge just enough of them) and index into the middle.
bruteForce.spaceComplexity: O(m+n) if fully merged, O(1) if merged only up to the midpoint

optimalApproach: Binary search over the partition index of the smaller array, using the 'left max <= right min on both sides' boundary condition to locate the correct overall partition in O(log(min(m,n))).
timeComplexity: O(log(min(m, n))) — binary search runs only over the smaller array's index range.
spaceComplexity: O(1) — only a few index/value variables, no copying.
followUps: Why must the binary search run over the smaller array, not either one arbitrarily?
Walk through what total_left represents and why it guarantees the correct overall split size.
